source_text: Ἐὰν μέν τοι πολλοὺς ἴδῃ συντρέχοντας τῷ ἐπαίνῳ, μεταβαλὼν πάλιν, βασκαίνει τῷ τεθνεῶτι. Τὸν πλοῦτον θαυμάζει μετὰ τὴν ἔκπτωσιν. Τὴν ὥραν τοῦ σώματος, ἢ τὴν ῥώμην καὶ τὴν εὐεξίαν μετὰ τὰς νόσους ἐπαινεῖ καὶ ἐξαίρει. Καὶ ὅλως, ἐχθρὸς μέν ἐστι τῶν παρόντων, φίλος δὲ τῶν ἀπολλυμένων. Τί ἂν οὖν γένοιτο τῆς νόσου ταύτης ὀλεθριώτερον; Φθορὰ τῆς ζωῆς, λύμη τῆς φύσεως, ἔχθρα τῶν παρὰ Θεοῦ δεδομένων ἡμῖν, ἐναντίωσις πρὸς Θεόν. Τί τὸν ἀρχέκακον δαίμονα εἰς τὸν κατὰ ἀνθρώπων ἐξέμηνε πόλεμον; Οὐχ ὁ φθόνος; δι' οὗ καὶ θεομάχος φανερῶς ἀπηλέγχθη, ἀχθόμενος μὲν Θεῷ ἐπὶ τῇ μεγαλοδωρεᾷ τῇ εἰς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, τὸν ἄνθρωπον δὲ ἀμυνόμενος, ἐπειδὴ Θεὸν οὐκ ἠδύνατο. Τὰ αὐτὰ δὲ ταῦτα ποιῶν καὶ ὁ Κάϊν δείκνυται, ὁ πρῶτος μαθητὴς τοῦ διαβό λου, καὶ φθόνον καὶ φόνον παρ' αὐτοῦ διδαχθεὶς, τὰς ἀδελφὰς ἀνομίας, ἃς καὶ Παῦλος συνέζευξεν, εἰπών· Μεστοὺς φθόνου, φόνου. Τί οὖν ἦν ὃ ἐποίησεν; Εἶδε τὴν παρὰ Θεοῦ τιμὴν, καὶ ἐξεκαύθη πρὸς ζῆλον, καὶ ἀνεῖλε τὸν τιμηθέντα, ἵνα καθάψηται τοῦ τιμή σαντος. Πρὸς γὰρ τὴν θεομαχίαν ἀδυνατῶν, εἰς ἀδελφοκτονίαν μετέπεσε. Φύγωμεν, ἀδελφοὶ, νόσον θεομαχίας διδάσκαλον, ἀνδροφονίας μητέρα, σύγχυσιν φύσεως, οἰκειότητος ἄγνοιαν, συμφορὰν ἀλογωτάτην. Τί λυπῇ, ἄνθρωπε, μηδὲν δεινὸν πεπονθώς; τί πολεμεῖς τῷ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς τισιν ὄντι, μηδὲν τῶν σῶν ἐλαττώσαντι; Ἐὰν δὲ δὴ καὶ εὐεργετούμενος ἀγανακτῇς, οὐκ ἄντικρυς τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ὠφελείας βα σκαίνεις; Ὁποῖος ἦν ὁ Σαοὺλ, ὃς τῶν εὐεργεσιῶν τὰς ὑπερβολὰς ἀφορμὴν τοῦ πολέμου τοῦ πρὸς τὸν Δαβὶδ ἐποιήσατο. Πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ, τῇ παναρμονίῳ ἐκείνῃ καὶ θείᾳ μουσικῇ τῆς μανίας ἀπαλλαγεὶς, ἐπειρᾶτο δόρατι διαπεῖραι τὸν εὐεργέτην· ἔπειτα σὺν αὐτῷ τῷ στρατῷ ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων περισωθεὶς, καὶ τῆς ἐπὶ τῷ Γολιὰθ αἰσχύνης ἀπαλλαγεὶς, ὅμως ἐπειδὴ ἐν τοῖς ἐπινικίοις τὸ δεκαπλάσιον τῆς τῶν συμβάντων αἰτίας τῷ Δαβὶδ ἀνέθεσαν αἱ χορεύουσαι· Ἐπάταξε Δαβὶδ ἐν μυριάσι, καὶ Σαοὺλ ἐν χιλιάσιν αὐτοῦ· διὰ μίαν ταύτην φωνὴν, καὶ τὴν ἐξ αὐτῆς τῆς ἀληθείας ὑπάρξασαν μαρτυρίαν, πρῶ τον αὐτόχειρ γενέσθαι, καὶ ἐξ ἐνέδρας ἀνελεῖν ἐπ εχείρησεν· εἶτα φυγάδα καταστήσας, οὐδὲ οὕτω τὴν ἔχθραν ἔστησεν, ἀλλὰ τὸ τελευταῖον ἐκστρατεύσας ἐπ' αὐτὸν τρισχιλίοις λογάσι, τὰς ἐρημίας διηρευνᾶτο. Εἰ δὲ ἠρωτήθη τοῦ πολέμου τὴν πρόφασιν, εἶπεν ἂν πάντως τὰς τοῦ ἀνδρὸς εὐποιίας. Ὅς γε παρ' αὐτὸν τὸν καιρὸν τῆς διώξεως καθεύδων καταληφθεὶς, ἕτοιμος εἰς σφαγὴν προκείμενος τῷ ἐχθρῷ, καὶ πάλιν περισωθεὶς ὑπὸ τοῦ δικαίου, ἐπαγαγεῖν αὐτῷ τὰς χεῖρας φυλαξαμένου, οὐδ' ὑπὸ ταύτης τῆς εὐεργεσίας ἐκάμφθη· ἀλλὰ καὶ πάλιν ἐστρατολόγει, καὶ πάλιν ἐδίωκεν· ἕως, καὶ δεύτερον ἁλοὺς ὑπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐν τῷ σπηλαίῳ, τοῦ μὲν τὴν ἀρετὴν λαμπροτέραν ἀπέδειξεν, ἑαυτοῦ δὲ τὴν πονηρίαν καταφανεστέραν ἐποίησε. Δυσμεταχειριστότατον ἔχθρας εἶδος ὁ φθόνος. Τοὺς μὲν γὰρ ἄλλως δυσμενεῖς ἡμερωτέρους ποιοῦσιν αἱ εὐποιίαι· τὸν βάσκανον δὲ καὶ κακοήθη τὸ καλῶς παθεῖν πλέον προσερεθίζει· καὶ ὅσῳπερ ἂν μειζόνων τύχῃ, μειζό νως ἀγανακτεῖ καὶ ἀνιᾶται, καὶ δυσχεραίνει. Πλεῖον γὰρ ἄχθεται τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ εὐεργέτου, ἢ χάριν ἔχει τοῖς εἰς αὐτὸν γινομένοις.
thought_title: Envy as the most destructive disease
orientation: Basil is describing how the envious person behaves toward the misfortunes of others, and now turns to show that envy is the most destructive passion, tracing it from the devil to Cain and Saul.
pass_a_gloss: If indeed he sees many running together to the praise, having changed again, he envies the dead man. He admires the wealth after the loss. He praises and exalts the bloom of the body, or the strength and the good condition, after the illnesses. And in general, he is an enemy of present things, but a friend of things being destroyed. What then could be more destructive than this disease? Corruption of life, ruin of nature, enmity toward the things given to us by God, opposition to God. What drove the arch-evil demon into the war against humans? Was it not envy? through which he was also clearly convicted as a fighter against God, grieving at God over the great gift to the human being, and defending himself against the human being, since he could not against God. And doing these same things Cain also is shown, the first disciple of the devil, having been taught by him both envy and murder, the sister lawless deeds, which Paul also yoked together, saying: Full of envy, murder. What then was it that he did? He saw the honor from God, and was inflamed to zeal, and killed the honored one, in order that he might lay hold of the one who honored. For being powerless against the fight against God, he fell into brother-murder. Let us flee, brothers, the disease that is the teacher of fighting against God, the mother of man-slaying, the confusion of nature, the ignorance of kinship, the most irrational calamity. Why are you grieved, human being, having suffered nothing terrible? Why do you make war on the one who is in some good things, who has diminished none of your things? But if indeed even while being benefited you are angry, are you not outright envying your own benefit? Of such a kind was Saul, who made the excesses of the benefits an occasion for the war against David. For first, having been released from the madness by that all-harmonious and divine music, he tried to pierce through with a spear the benefactor; then having been saved together with the army itself from the enemies, and having been released from the shame over Goliath, nevertheless since in the victory songs the dancing women attributed the tenfold of the cause of the events to David: David struck in ten thousands, and Saul in his thousands; because of this one voice, and the testimony that came from the truth itself, he attempted first to become a murderer with his own hand, and to kill from ambush; then having made him a fugitive, not even so did he stop the enmity, but finally having marched out against him with three thousand chosen men, he searched through the deserts. But if he had been asked the pretext of the war, he would have said altogether the good deeds of the man. Who indeed at the very time of the pursuit, having been caught sleeping, lying ready for slaughter before the enemy, and again having been saved by the just man, who guarded against bringing his hands upon him, was not bent even by this benefit; but again he was enlisting soldiers, and again he was pursuing; until, having been caught a second time by the same man in the cave, he made the virtue of the one more brilliant, and made his own wickedness more evident. Envy is the most difficult kind of enmity to manage. For benefits make those who are otherwise hostile gentler; but the envious and malicious person, being treated well provokes more; and by however much greater things he happens upon, by so much more he is angry and grieved and vexed. For he is more grieved at the power of the benefactor than he has gratitude for the things done to him.

Literal compound rendering preserves the force of the Greek compound, parallel to 'man-slaying' for ἀνδροφονία.
Literal rendering of the compound adjective; 'arch-evil' keeps the prefix force without importing a standard English term.
The metaphor of envy and murder as sisters is preserved literally.

pass_b_english: But if he sees many people joining in the praise, he changes course again and envies the dead man. He admires the wealth after it has been lost. He praises and exalts the beauty of the body, or its strength and vigor, after illness has come. In short, he is an enemy of what is present and a friend of what is perishing. What could be more destructive than this disease? It is the corruption of life, the ruin of nature, hostility toward the gifts God has given us, opposition to God. What drove the arch-evil demon into his war against humanity? Was it not envy? Through it he was openly exposed as a fighter against God—grieving at God for the great gift given to man, and taking vengeance on man because he could not reach God. Cain is shown doing the very same things: the devil's first disciple, taught by him both envy and murder, the kindred lawless deeds that Paul also joined together when he said, "full of envy, murder" (Romans 1:29). What then did Cain do? He saw the honor given by God, and he burned with envy, and he killed the one who was honored, so that he might strike at the one who gave the honor. Unable to fight against God, he fell into brother-murder. Let us flee, brothers, from a disease that teaches fighting against God, that is the mother of man-slaying, the confusion of nature, the forgetting of kinship, the most irrational of disasters. Why are you grieved, man, when you have suffered nothing terrible? Why do you make war on someone who has good things, who has diminished nothing of yours? And if you are angered even while receiving benefits, are you not plainly envying your own advantage? Such was Saul, who made the excess of benefits the occasion for his war against David. First, after being freed from madness by that all-harmonious and divine music, he tried to pierce his benefactor with a spear. Then, after being saved together with his army from the enemies, and freed from the shame over Goliath, still—because in the victory songs the dancing women attributed to David ten times the credit for what had happened: "David struck down his ten thousands, and Saul his thousands"—because of this one phrase, and the testimony that came from the truth itself, he first tried to become his murderer with his own hand and to kill him from ambush. Then, after making him a fugitive, he did not even so put an end to his hatred, but finally marched out against him with three thousand chosen men and searched the deserts. If he had been asked the reason for the war, he would certainly have said: the man's good deeds. For at the very time of the pursuit, when he was caught sleeping and lay ready for slaughter before his enemy, and was again saved by the righteous man, who guarded against laying hands on him, he was not softened even by this benefit. But again he gathered an army, and again he pursued—until, caught a second time by the same man in the cave, he made David's virtue shine more brightly and made his own wickedness more evident. Envy is the most difficult kind of enmity to manage. For benefits make those who are hostile for other reasons gentler; but the envious and malicious person is provoked further by being treated well. And the greater the benefits he receives, the more he is angered and grieved and annoyed. He is more burdened by the power of his benefactor than grateful for what is done for him.

problems.why: ἀδελφάς means 'sister' but here means 'kindred/related' crimes; 'sister lawless deeds' is nonsensical in English.

problems.quote: the tenfold share of the cause of what had happened
problems.source_quote: τὸ δεκαπλάσιον τῆς τῶν συμβάντων αἰτίας
problems.why: αἰτίας here means 'credit/attribution', not 'cause'. The women gave David tenfold the credit.
problems.fix: ten times the credit for what had happened
problems.ruling: αἰτίας here means 'credit' not 'cause'; 'tenfold share of the cause' misleads the reader.

edits.old: the tenfold share of the cause of what had happened
edits.new: ten times the credit for what had happened

fixed: Changed 'the sister lawless deeds' to 'the kindred lawless deeds' because ἀδελφάς here means 'kindred/related', not literally 'sister'.
Changed 'the tenfold share of the cause of what had happened' to 'ten times the credit for what had happened' because αἰτίας here means 'credit/attribution', not 'cause'.

last_rejected.why: ἀδελφάς here means 'akin/akin to each other' (envy and murder are sister vices), not 'kindred lawless deeds' which is awkward and unclear.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Kindred lawless deeds' accurately renders τὰς ἀδελφὰς ἀνομίας; ἀδελφός can mean 'akin/sister' in Greek, and 'kindred' captures this relationship between envy and murder as paired vices.

last_rejected.quote: when he said, "full of envy, murder" (Romans 1:29)
last_rejected.why: English hides that Paul is the quoted speaker with 'when he said'; Greek εἰπών clearly marks Paul's speech.
last_rejected.fix: saying, 'full of envy, murder' (Romans 1:29), or: in the words of Paul, 'full of envy, murder'
last_rejected.ruling: εἰπών means 'saying'; English 'when he said' correctly attributes speech to Paul. No meaning lost.

last_rejected.why: ἀλογωτάτην means 'most irrational/unreasonable' but συμφορὰν means 'misfortune/calamity', not 'disaster'; 'disaster' is too strong and changes tone.
last_rejected.ruling: συμφορά includes 'disaster/calamity/misfortune'; 'disaster' is within normal range. Not a major error.

last_rejected.why: πρὸς ζῆλον means 'with jealousy/zeal', not 'with envy'; ζῆλος is distinct from φθόνος. Though ζῆλος can mean envy, here it's likely 'jealousy/zeal' in a negative sense, but 'envy' conflates the terms.
last_rejected.ruling: ζῆλος can mean 'envy/jealousy'; in context of Cain's φθόνος, 'envy' is within normal range. Mere preference.

last_rejected.why: δύναμις here means 'power/ability' but in context of Saul/David, it refers to David's military success/popularity; 'power' is too abstract and misses the specific sense of capability/superiority that provokes envy.
last_rejected.ruling: δύναμις means 'power/might'; 'power' is standard. Contextual nuance is preference, not major error.
